I'll start by reading the task file.

# Your task (after reading)

You are a student reader helping an editor test a teaching article before it is published.
Work only inside this directory. Do not search the web. Be honest: the editor needs to know
where the article fails to teach.

1. Read `article.md` from start to finish. The series has a glossary, `glossary.md`; look terms up there as a reader would, and report in your feedback only terms that neither the article nor the glossary explains.
2. Answer the questions in its "Check your understanding" section. Write the answers to
   `answers.md`, numbered like the questions. Two to six sentences each, in your own words; show
   working where a question asks for a calculation or a translation. After each answer add a line
   `Confidence: N` with N from 1 (guessing) to 5 (certain).
3. Write `feedback.md` with these sections:
   - **Passages I had to read twice**: quote each (one or two sentences) and say what was unclear.
   - **Terms used before they were explained, or never explained**: one line each.
   - **Claims I could not verify from the article itself**: quote each and say what evidence or
     step is missing.
   - **Section scores**: for each numbered section, a score from 1 (lost) to 5 (clear) and one
     sentence of reason.
   - **Questions that the article did not let me answer**: which quiz questions, if any, could not
     be answered from the text, and what was missing.
   - **One thing to add and one thing to cut**.
4. Write `diary.md`: a work diary of this session in the format of `diary-format.md`, with one
   step for reading, one for the quiz and one for the feedback. Record what was hard.

Finish by replying with one line: DONE.

# 10. Architecture and a Roadmap

The previous articles each examined one part of the system. This one puts the parts together. It takes stock of what the firmware now contains, describes four structural changes that the earlier articles imply but did not develop, and then orders all of the proposed work by cost, risk and what each step makes possible. By the end you should be able to say how many execution mechanisms the device carries and which could go, explain why one description of the reactor's functions should generate the three lists that are now written by hand, state what a typed binary screen protocol would replace, and defend an order of work from the evidence in this issue.

The article uses the vocabulary of the whole issue; every term is in the glossary. The most frequent are these. A *world* is one scheduled program, and the *nucleus* is the kernel that runs worlds. An *engine* executes a world's code: QuickJS interprets JavaScript, WAMR interprets WebAssembly, and the native loader runs RV32 machine code from ELF files. CJI is the project's first compiler, for unannotated JavaScript; the *typed compiler* is the second, for a small language with declared types. A *reactor* is the prebuilt C module through which a compiled application calls the system.

## 10.1 What the firmware contains

After two days of rapid work the device carries more machinery than any one design would have chosen.

| Component | Role | Size or extent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Runs JavaScript worlds; also runs the typed compiler | Part of the base firmware |
| WAMR | Runs WebAssembly worlds | Part of the base firmware |
| Native loader | Loads RV32 ELF modules | Small |
| CJI runtime | Dynamic values, strings and a garbage collector for CJI-compiled worlds | Linked into the firmware |
| CJI compiler tool | CJI itself, compiled to RV32, for compiling on the device | about 660 kB in the image; relocated at boot |
| Typed compiler | Frontend, WebAssembly linker, RV32 lowering | 43 kB of JavaScript source |
| Shared typed reactor | Connects a fully typed application to the nucleus | 508 lines of C |
| Per-application reactors | Hold the parts of Agenda and Files that are not yet typed | 869 and 334 lines of C |
| Compositor | The world that draws every screen | 485 lines of JavaScript, compiled by CJI for the firmware |

That is three engines, two compilers, a run-time system that exists only for the first compiler's output, and three reactors. Each was a reasonable step. Together they are a cost in flash, in boot time and in the number of things a maintainer must understand.

A second inventory is as telling. The Editor exists twice: as 316 lines of JavaScript, which is the original and the reference for tests, and as about 1,730 lines of typed source. Agenda is 307 lines of JavaScript, and its typed version is 468 lines of typed source plus 869 lines of C. The typed versions are four to six times longer than the programs they replace: a factor of 5.5 for Editor, and 4.4 for Agenda when its C reactor is counted. The difference is the price of the language's missing features: no allocation, no string operations beyond single code units, and no `await` (Articles 8 and 9). With twelve applications still to port, that multiplier is the main argument for extending the language before porting further.

## 10.2 One description of the reactor's functions

A typed application reaches the system through 28 functions that the shared reactor provides. Each is currently declared in three places that must agree.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I["One interface description (proposed)"] -.-> A
    I -.-> B
    I -.-> C
    A["compiler/typed-world.js: name, parameter types, result type, in order"]
    B["sdk/typed/rv32-slot.S: one jump per function, in the same order"]
    C["sdk/typed/world.c: the C implementation of each function"]
    A --- B --- C
```

The compiler's table gives each function's name and types and fixes its position. The assembly file lists one trampoline per function in the same order; native code calls function number *k* by jumping to the *k*-th entry. The C file implements them. The number of functions is also stored in a header at the start of the reactor's code area, and the linker compares it with the length of the compiler's table. That check catches a function added to one list and not the other. It cannot catch two lists of the same length in different orders. If the order in the first two files ever differs, calls go to the wrong function with arguments of the wrong meaning, and no check detects it.

The remedy is an **interface description**: one file that states, for each function, its name, parameter types and result type, from which a build step generates the compiler's table, the trampolines and the C prototypes. If the JavaScript version of the reactor proposed in section 10.4 is built, its function list is generated from the same file. This is ordinary practice wherever two languages meet. The WebAssembly Component Model's interface language, WIT, is a current example and has a useful property for this system: it can declare a *resource* type, an entity "that can only be passed around indirectly via handle values", with owned and borrowed handles. Handle types of that kind would express whether a handle argument is consumed or only lent (Article 9). Two further facts that Articles 7 and 9 need for each function are not part of WIT and would be this project's own additions to the description: which capability the function requires, and how much fuel, the counter that bounds a handler's running time, a call should be charged.

This change is small, and it is a precondition for growing the set of reactor functions safely, which every ported application will require.

## 10.3 A typed screen protocol

Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the path to the screen, and noted that in the measured firmware it was already native code. The cost lies in what the compositor is asked to do. It is worth following one screen update through the system as it works today.

1. The application builds a description of its screen as JSON text. In the typed language this is done by writing string fragments into a buffer one after another; Editor contains 104 such `writeLiteral` calls, for instance `output.writeLiteral(at, ",\"color\":\"accent\"}")`.
2. The reactor converts the buffer from UTF-16 to UTF-8, escaping characters as JSON requires. The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step.
3. The nucleus copies the message to the compositor's queue. A message is limited to 16 KiB. (This step would remain with any protocol.)
4. The compositor parses the JSON text into a tree of dynamically typed objects, which are allocated on a garbage-collected heap.
5. The compositor walks the tree, computes positions, and draws. (This step is the compositor's actual job and would remain.)

Steps 1, 2 and 4 exist only because the two sides exchange text. The figure of six bytes per unit in step 2 is from the Editor's capacity design note in the project's records. Both sides know the structure in advance: a screen is a list of rows, each with a style, an indentation and a run of characters.

A **typed binary protocol** states that structure once, as record layouts, and both sides use it directly. The application writes fields at fixed offsets, which the typed language already does for its own records. The compositor reads the same fields at the same offsets. Nothing is formatted, escaped or parsed, and nothing is allocated to hold a tree. A full Editor screen is 17 rows of at most 49 characters. As 16-bit code units that is 833 × 2 = 1,666 bytes of text, and with a four-byte header per row for style, indentation and length, 1,734 bytes in all.

The layouts belong in the interface description of section 10.2, so that the application's compiler and the compositor are generated from the same source and cannot disagree.

The natural companion is a compositor written in the typed language. The compositor is today 485 lines of JavaScript compiled by CJI, with CJI's run-time system behind it. A typed compositor would have no garbage collector and no dynamic values, and it is the one world whose speed every other world's responsiveness depends on.

This is the largest single piece of work proposed in this issue, and it rests on a hypothesis. It should be started only if the key-to-pixel measurement of Article 2 confirms that the compositor dominates.

## 10.4 One source for both engines

When the typed compiler fails or is disabled, the firmware falls back to the original JavaScript application. Every ported application is therefore maintained in two forms, and the two can drift apart. The tests rely on the JavaScript original as the definition of correct behaviour, which is appropriate during a port and becomes a burden afterwards.

The typed source looks like JavaScript with annotations. Could QuickJS run it directly? Two developments in the JavaScript world suggest the shape of an answer.

The first is **asm.js**, a strict subset of JavaScript designed as a compilation target. Its insight was that type information can be written in valid JavaScript: a parameter is given the type *integer* "by means of an explicit coercion on function entry", written `x = x|0`, and a floating-point type by `x = +x` [Herman et al. 2014]. Code in this style runs unchanged in any JavaScript engine and can also be compiled ahead of time using plain machine integers. Because asm.js is a subset of JavaScript, an asm.js program means exactly what JavaScript says it means. The asm.js specification adds only the rules for recognizing which programs are in the subset.

The second is **erasable type syntax**. TypeScript 5.8 added an option that rejects every TypeScript construct with run-time behaviour, so that what remains can be turned into JavaScript by deleting the annotations, and a proposal before the JavaScript standards committee would have engines ignore annotations as if they were comments. That proposal is at stage 1 of the committee's process, which means it is under consideration and nothing has been accepted.

For the typed language, deletion alone is not enough, because its semantics differ from JavaScript's in specific, enumerable ways.

| Construct | Typed language | JavaScript after deleting annotations | What a JavaScript emitter must add |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `a + b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | 64-bit floating point | `(a + b) | 0` |
| `a * b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | May lose low bits above 2⁵³ | `Math.imul(a, b)` |
| `a / b` on `i32` | Truncates; traps on zero | Fractional result; infinity on zero | A checked helper |
| `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of range | Traps | Returns NaN | A wrapper class with a checked method |
| `record` declarations | Fixed layout in memory | Not JavaScript | An object or typed array |

Each row is a mechanical rewrite. A third, small backend that emits JavaScript with these rewrites, together with a JavaScript implementation of the reactor's 28 functions, would let QuickJS execute the same typed source. The project's device-language study considered compiling the typed language to JavaScript as the way to *run applications fast*, and rejected it for that purpose, because the interpreter would still treat every number as a general value. The two purposes proposed here do not depend on speed.

- **One source per application.** After a port is accepted, the JavaScript original can be retired. The fallback is the same program in another engine.
- **A reference for the compiler.** The JavaScript emitter is a second, independent implementation of the language's semantics. Running an application through both and comparing screens is a test of the WebAssembly and RV32 backends that needs no hand-written original.

One limit should be stated. A reference derived from the same source cannot reveal an error in the source's logic. During a port, the original JavaScript application remains the standard of behaviour.

## 10.5 Fewer engines

Which mechanisms of section 10.1 are needed in the long run depends on the outcome of earlier articles' proposals.

| Component | Needed as long as | Could be removed when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Unported JavaScript worlds exist; it also hosts the typed compiler and the interactive console | Not in view; it is the system's base |
| WAMR | Typed applications from untrusted source must be confined | The verifier of Article 7 exists and is trusted, and no foreign WebAssembly modules are wanted |
| CJI runtime | Any CJI-compiled world ships, which today includes the compositor and the drivers | Those worlds are ported to the typed language |
| CJI compiler tool on the device | Compiling unannotated JavaScript on the device remains a goal | Now, by giving up that goal. Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively, and it costs 660 kB and a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around |
| Per-application reactors | Agenda and Files keep logic in C | Those applications are fully typed |

The clearest decision is the fourth row. CJI remains valuable as a workstation compiler that turns existing JavaScript worlds into native code for the firmware image, and the techniques of Article 4 would improve it in that role. As the compiler that runs on the device, it has been superseded by the typed compiler.

## 10.6 The roadmap

The table gathers every proposal in this issue. Effort is a rough class: small is days, medium is one to two weeks, large is more. "Unlocks" names what becomes possible afterwards.

| # | Step | Effort | Risk | Unlocks | Article |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 0 | Measure key press to pixels, and per-world time for one key press | small | low | Every later decision | 2 |
| 1 | Cache compiled modules under a content key | small | low | Removes 2–3 s from every boot | 6 |
| 2 | Take the CJI tool off the device | small | low | 660 kB of flash; simpler boot | 10 |
| 3 | Interface description for reactor functions | small | low | Safe growth of the reactor; data for steps 6 and 8 | 10 |
| 4 | Language: enumerations, distinct integers, guard facts for bounds checks, a report of reactor usage per world, `else`, `for`, `break`, forward calls with a cycle check | small each | low | Shorter, safer typed sources; fewer checks | 9 |
| 5 | RV32 backend with a compile-time operand stack | medium | medium | Native code about 2.7 times smaller; memory headroom | 5 |
| 6 | Fuel counter, static stack bound, output verifier | medium | medium | Native code from untrusted source | 7 |
| 7 | `await` compiled to state machines | medium to large | medium | Ports without hand-written continuations | 8 |
| 8 | Per-turn arena with its lifetime rules | medium | medium | Applications that allocate | 9 |
| 9 | JavaScript emitter and reactor shim | medium | low | One source per application; a compiler reference | 10 |
| 10 | Typed screen protocol and typed compositor | large | depends on step 0 | Faster path to the screen for every world | 10 |
| 11 | Experiment: worlds in user mode under PMP, the processor's memory protection | medium | high | Confinement of any native code | 7 |
| 12 | Linear handles, then typestate | medium to large | medium | Compile-time checking of grants and releases | 9 |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["0 Measure"] --> S10["10 Screen protocol and compositor"]
    S0 --> S5["5 Better RV32 backend"]
    S1["1 Cache"]
    S2["2 CJI tool off the device"]
    S3["3 Interface description"] --> S6["6 Fuel, stack bound, verifier"]
    S3 --> S8["8 Per-turn arena"]
    S3 --> S9["9 JavaScript emitter and reactor shim"]
    S3 --> S10
    S4["4 Small language additions"] --> S7["7 await"]
    S5 --> S6
    S7 --> S8
    S7 --> P["Port the remaining twelve applications"]
    S8 --> P
    S8 --> S12["12 Linear handles, typestate"]
    S6 --> W["WAMR becomes optional"]
    S11["11 PMP experiment"]
```

An arrow means that the later step needs the earlier one. Steps without arrows into them can start at any time. Three features of the ordering deserve a sentence each. Steps 0 to 4 are small and low-risk and do not depend on one another; they come first, with the measurement of step 0 run early because the larger steps 5 and 10 wait on its result. Step 7 comes before the remaining ports because of the multiplier of section 10.1: porting twelve applications in the current style would produce a great deal of code that `await` would then make obsolete. Step 10 is deliberately late and conditional.

## 10.7 Predictions that would falsify the plan

A plan built on measurements should say what further measurements would refute it. Each of the following is a specific, checkable prediction that follows from an article of this issue. Where the article gave a number, it is repeated here; where it gave only a direction, a threshold is set here so that the prediction can fail.

| Prediction | Check | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files, where today there are 1,529 (Article 5) | Implement it for Files first and count | The counting model is wrong; re-examine before doing Editor |
| Application code is under 10 percent of key press to pixels (Article 2's rough model gives under 5 percent of the measured part) | Step 0 | Raise the priority of step 5 for the affected application |
| With a cache, an unedited Editor costs under 100 ms at boot instead of 2–3 s (Article 6 expects 14 ms to load plus tens of milliseconds to hash) | Time a boot with a warm cache | Look at hashing and load costs |
| A verifier accepts all code the new backend emits and rejects that code after random single-bit changes, or the changed code can do no harm (Article 7, section 7.6) | Mutation testing of emitted modules | Find which property the accepted harmful module violates and add the missing check |
| The `await` transformation reproduces Editor's behaviour using no more than its current 71 state fields (Article 8, section 8.6) | Rewrite Editor's open and search paths with `await` and compare screens | Saving every variable that is live across a wait is less economical than hand-written state; examine which variables it saves that the hand-written code does not |

## 10.8 Key points

- The firmware carries three engines, two compilers, a run-time system for the first compiler's output, and three reactors. The typed ports are four to six times longer than the JavaScript they replace.
- The reactor's 28 functions are listed by hand in three files that must agree in order. One interface description should generate all three.
- Screen updates are exchanged as JSON text that one side formats and the other parses into garbage-collected objects. A typed binary protocol removes both steps; it should be built only if measurement confirms that the compositor dominates.
- A JavaScript emitter for the typed language would give one source per application and an independent reference for the compiler.
- The CJI tool should leave the device now. WAMR can become optional once native code can be verified.
- Small, low-risk steps come first; `await` comes before the remaining ports; the compositor work waits for evidence.

## 10.9 Check your understanding

1. The reactor's header stores the number of reactor functions, and the linker checks it. Which mistake does that check catch, which does it miss, and how does the proposed interface description remove both?
2. Of the five steps of a screen update in section 10.3, which three exist only because the two sides exchange text, and why do the other two remain under a binary protocol?
3. Why is deleting type annotations not sufficient to make typed source run correctly in a JavaScript engine? Give two specific constructs and what must be added for each.
4. A JavaScript emitter gives a reference implementation derived from the same source. What kind of error can it detect, and what kind can it not?
5. Why does the roadmap place `await` before porting the remaining applications? Use the figures of section 10.1 in your answer.
6. Choose one prediction from section 10.7 and state what observation would refute it and what the plan says to do then.

# Glossary

Each term is defined as it is used in this issue. The number in brackets is the article that introduces it.

## The system

**Claim** [1]. An entry in the system's manifest stating that a world may open a given kind of hardware or a given directory. The nucleus checks every such use against the world's claims.

**Compositor** [1]. The world that owns the screen. Applications send it a description of their screen; it lays the description out and draws it.

**Engine** [1]. The mechanism that executes a world's code. There are three: QuickJS (JavaScript), WAMR (WebAssembly) and native (RV32 machine code).

**Handle** [9]. A number that stands for an open file or a granted permission. Authority is exercised by presenting a handle to the nucleus.

**Manifest** [1]. The file that lists the system's worlds with their engines, memory limits, turn budgets and claims.

**Nucleus** [1]. The kernel, written in C. It schedules worlds, delivers messages and checks claims.

**Reactor** [1]. A prebuilt C module shipped in the firmware that connects a compiled application to the nucleus. Compiled code is copied into a reserved place inside it. The *shared typed reactor* serves any fully typed application.

**Slot** [5, 7]. Two meanings, distinguished by context. A *frame slot* is a fixed position in a function's stack frame. *The slot* in a reactor is the contiguous region reserved for an application's compiled RV32 code.

**Split-phase operation** [8]. An operation with a request that returns at once and a completion delivered later as a separate event.

**Token** [8]. A number returned when a split-phase operation is started and carried by the event that completes it.

**Trampoline** [7]. A fixed single-jump entry at the start of the reactor's slot, one per reactor function. Compiled native code calls reactor function *k* by jumping to the *k*-th trampoline.

**Trap** [1]. An immediate fault that ends a world's turn, raised for example by an out-of-range index or a division by zero.

**Turn** [1]. The handling of one event by one world.

**Turn budget** [1]. The longest time one uninterrupted piece of a turn may run. A world that overruns is stopped.

**World** [1]. One scheduled program: an application, a driver or a service, with its own memory limit and turn budget.

## The compilers

**CJI** [1]. The first compiler: it accepts unannotated JavaScript, infers types over the whole program, and emits RV32 machine code. Named after the book *Compiling JavaScript, Incrementally*.

**Demotion** [3]. In CJI, replacing an operation provisionally compiled as integer arithmetic by general floating-point arithmetic when the range proof fails.

**Library specialization** [3]. In CJI, generating a separate copy of a library routine for each call site, specialized to the types used there. Called *customization* in the Self literature.

**Lowering** [1, 5]. Translating a program from a higher-level form to a lower-level one; here, WebAssembly to RV32.

**Typed compiler** [1]. The second compiler: it accepts a small JavaScript-like language with declared types, emits WebAssembly in one pass, and optionally lowers that to RV32.

**Typed language** [1]. The source language of the typed compiler, with the types `i32`, `bool`, `string`, `buffer` and `record`.

## Program analysis

**Abstract interpretation** [3]. The general theory of analyses that compute approximate facts about all executions of a program by iterating over an ordered set of facts.

**Constraint graph** [4]. A graph with a node for each value and an edge wherever one value's facts feed another's.

**Dense and sparse analysis** [4]. A dense analysis keeps facts for every variable at every program point. A sparse analysis attaches each fact to the definition of a value and propagates it only to that value's uses.

**Demand-driven analysis** [4]. An analysis that starts from a question (for example, "is this check redundant?") and computes only what is needed to answer it.

**Fixpoint** [3]. The state of an iterative analysis in which a further visit to the program changes nothing.

**Join** [3]. The operation that combines the facts arriving at a control-flow merge. For ranges, the join of [0, 3] and [2, 9] is [0, 9].

**Jump function** [4]. For one argument of one call, a small expression giving the argument's value in terms of the enclosing function's own parameters. A form of summary.

**Liveness** [8]. A variable is live at a point if some path from that point reads it before writing it.

**Local checking** [4]. Checking and compiling a function from its own text and the declared signatures of what it calls, with no facts about its callers.

**Range (interval)** [3]. The smallest and largest value a variable can take, in CJI with flags for fraction, negative zero and NaN.

**SSA form** [4]. Static single-assignment form: a program representation in which every variable is assigned in exactly one place, with φ-functions selecting between definitions at merges. *Extended* SSA adds a renaming (π) on each outcome of a branch.

**Strongly connected component** [4]. A maximal group of nodes in a graph that all depend on each other through cycles.

**Summary** [4]. A compact description of how a function's outputs depend on its inputs.

**Whole-program inference** [3]. Solving for types or other facts using every function and every call in the program.

**Widening** [3]. Jumping a bound that keeps moving to a much larger value so that iteration terminates, at some cost in precision.

## Code generation

**Back-edge** [7]. The jump from the end of a loop body back to the loop's start.

**Branch over a jump** [5]. A conditional branch that skips an unconditional jump, used where the distance to the target is not known to be short.

**Compile-time operand stack** [5]. A list kept by the compiler during translation that records where each operand-stack value currently is: in a register, a known constant, the current value of a local, or a pending comparison. Also called a value stack, a virtual stack, or static stack caching.

**Flush** [5]. Moving every pending entry of the compile-time operand stack to a fixed, agreed location before control flow splits or merges, or before a call.

**Frame** [5]. A function's private area of memory on the stack. In Article 8, also the fixed group of persistent fields that holds an asynchronous function's saved state.

**Join (control flow)** [5]. A point in the code reached from two or more paths.

# Answers to "Check your understanding"

## 1.

The header stores only a count, and the linker compares that count with the length of
the compiler's table in `compiler/typed-world.js`. It therefore catches a function that
was added to one of those two lists and not the other: the numbers no longer match.
What it cannot catch is any mistake that keeps the length the same — above all two lists
of equal length written in a different order. In that case native code calling function
number *k* jumps to the *k*-th trampoline, which is now a different function, so it runs
the wrong code with arguments that mean something else, and no check fires. Nothing in
the article says how the third file, `sdk/typed/world.c`, is checked at all, so its order
is unchecked today as well. The interface description removes both failures at the root:
the compiler's table, the trampolines and the C prototypes are all *generated* from one
file, so there is only one list and one order, and a disagreement has nowhere to arise.

Confidence: 4

## 2.

Of the five steps, the three that exist only because the two sides exchange *text* are
step 1 (the application writes a JSON description of its screen into a buffer with
`writeLiteral` calls), step 2 (the reactor converts that buffer from UTF-16 to UTF-8 and
escapes it as JSON requires) and step 4 (the compositor parses the JSON text into a tree
of dynamically typed objects on a garbage-collected heap). Step 3, the nucleus copying
the message into the compositor's queue, remains because two separate worlds still have
to hand data over; the article says explicitly that this step "would remain with any
protocol". Step 5, walking the structure, computing positions and drawing, is the
compositor's actual job and is needed whatever the data looks like. Under a binary
protocol the application writes fields at fixed offsets and the compositor reads the same
offsets, so steps 1, 2 and 4 collapse into one store and one load: nothing is formatted,
escaped or parsed, and no tree is allocated.

Confidence: 5

## 3.

Deleting annotations leaves JavaScript code whose meaning differs from the typed
language in specific places, so a plain deleter produces a program that computes the
wrong answers rather than a compile error. Two examples from the article's table. First,
`a + b` on `i32` must wrap at 32 bits, but JavaScript `+` is 64-bit floating point, so the
emitter must add `(a + b) | 0` to force the result back into 32 bits. Second, `a * b` on
`i32` wraps at 32 bits, whereas a JavaScript product can lose low bits above 2^53, so the
emitter must emit `Math.imul(a, b)` instead. The article gives three more of the same
kind: division must become a checked helper because the typed language truncates and
traps on zero while JavaScript returns a fraction or infinity, `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of
range traps in the typed language but returns NaN in JavaScript so it needs a wrapper
class with a checked method, and `record` declarations have a fixed memory layout that
has to become an object or a typed array.

Confidence: 5

## 4.

Because the emitter is a second, independent implementation of the typed language's
semantics, running one application through the JavaScript path and through the WebAssembly
or RV32 path and comparing the resulting screens tests *the backends*: any place where the
WebAssembly or RV32 code behaves differently from the language definition shows up as a
different screen. What it cannot detect is an error in the source program's own logic. If
the typed source is wrong, both emitters reproduce the same wrong behaviour, and the two
screens agree while the application is still broken. That is why the article keeps the
hand-written JavaScript original as the standard of behaviour during a port; the emitter
may only replace it after the port has been accepted. Similar logic covers a mistake in
the emitter itself: since the emitter is new code, an error there would also produce a
mismatch, and the article does not say how the two kinds of mismatch would be told apart.

Confidence: 4

## 5.

The roadmap puts `await` (step 7) before the remaining ports because of the multiplier in
section 10.1. There the typed versions are measured as 4 to 6 times longer than the
programs they replace: Editor is 316 lines of JavaScript against about 1,730 lines of
typed source, that is 1,730 / 316 = 5.5, and Agenda is 307 lines of JavaScript against
468 lines of typed source plus 869 lines of C, that is (468 + 869) / 307 = 1,337 / 307 =
4.4. Twelve applications are still to be ported, so porting them in the current style
would multiply roughly 4 to 5 times their JavaScript size into new typed source and new C.
`await` is named as one of the missing features that cause that length, and Article 8's
alternative is hand-written continuations moved into persistent state, which is exactly
the kind of code that `await` would make obsolete. Writing twelve applications that way
first would therefore produce a large body of code that has to be rewritten afterwards.

Confidence: 4

## 6.

Take the first prediction: "A compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files,
where today there are 1,529". The stated check is to implement the new backend for Files
first and count the emitted instructions. The prediction is refuted if that count comes
out well above 593 and near or above today's 1,529, since the claimed saving would then
not exist. The article's response in that case is to treat the counting model used in
Article 5 as wrong and to re-examine it before starting on Editor. Note that the two
numbers given here also fail to produce the "about 2.7 times smaller" figure of step 5:
1,529 / 593 = 2.58, so a reader cannot reproduce the 2.7 from this table.

Confidence: 5

1. "The number of functions is also stored in a header at the start of the reactor's code
   area, and the linker compares it with the length of the compiler's table. That check
   catches a function added to one list and not the other."

   work out which two: presumably the header count comes from the assembly file (one
   trampoline per function) and is compared with the compiler's table. That is never
   stated, and the C file's order is left completely unchecked with no comment. It also
   says "the linker" here where the diagram promises a "build step" for the generated
   files, which is a different actor.

2. "Two further facts that Articles 7 and 9 need for each function are not part of WIT and
   would be this project's own additions to the description: which capability the function
   requires, and how much fuel, the counter that bounds a handler's running time, a call
   should be charged."
   — Four clauses are nested inside one another, and the second list item hides its own
   apposition in the middle. I had to unpack it into "…and how much fuel a call should be
   charged, where fuel is the counter that bounds a handler's running time".

3. "A full Editor screen is 17 rows of at most 49 characters. As 16-bit code units that is
   833 × 2 = 1,666 bytes of text, and with a four-byte header per row for style,
   indentation and length, 1,734 bytes in all."
   — The arithmetic works (17 × 49 = 833, 833 × 2 = 1,666, plus 17 × 4 = 68 gives 1,734),
   but the field widths are never given, so the reader cannot see how three fields fit in
   four bytes. I had to guess one byte for style, one for indentation and two for length.

4. "Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the
   path to the screen, and noted that in the measured firmware it was already native code.
   The cost lies in what the compositor is asked to do."
   — These sentences pull against each other until section 10.3's step list explains it. If
   the compositor is already native code, the reader's first guess is that there is no time
   left to win; only later does the article say the lost time is the JSON parsing and the
   garbage-collected tree, not the drawing.

5. "It takes stock of what the firmware now contains, describes four structural changes that
   the earlier articles imply but did not develop…"
   — The count of four never reappears, so the reader must decide which sections count.
   10.2, 10.3 and 10.4 are clearly changes; 10.5 ("Fewer engines") reads as a consequence
   of the others and contains no new structure, and section 10.3 in fact contains two
   proposals (the protocol and the typed compositor). Four is plausible but not obvious.

6. In the section 10.5 table, the row for the on-device CJI compiler reads "Needed as long
   as … Compiling unannotated JavaScript on the device remains a goal" and then, under
   "Could be removed when", "Now, by giving up that goal."
   — The column headings are about a condition that will happen in the future, and the
   entry is an argument, not a condition. It took a second reading to see that the table
   is saying the row can be removed by a decision rather than by finishing other work.

7. "The `await` transformation reproduces Editor's behaviour using no more than its current
   71 state fields" … "If it fails … Saving every variable that is live across a wait is
   less economical than hand-written state; examine which variables it saves that the
   hand-written code does not."
   — "71 state fields" and "the counting model" in the first row both refer to work in
   Articles 5 and 8 that this article does not summarise, so a reader who is reading this
   article alone cannot judge whether the prediction is generous or strict.

## Terms used before they were explained, or never explained

- **firmware** — used in the first sentence ("what the firmware now contains") and never
  defined in the article or in the glossary, though most later sections depend on it.
- **ELF** (section 10.1, "Loads RV32 ELF modules") — not explained anywhere; only the
  glossary's *Engine* entry hints that native means RV32 machine code.
- **capability** (section 10.2, "which capability the function requires") — not in the
  glossary. *Claim* is close but is defined as a manifest entry, and it is not said whether
  the two are the same thing.
- **relocation** (section 10.5, "a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around") —
  never explained, although it is one of the costs used to argue for removing the CJI tool.
- **garbage collector / garbage-collected heap** — used in section 10.3 ("allocated on a
  garbage-collected heap") and in the 10.1 table; the glossary mentions "a garbage
  collector" inside the *CJI runtime* entry without defining what one does.
- **mutation testing** (section 10.7, "Mutation testing of emitted modules") — never
  explained; the reader must infer that it means changing emitted code deliberately and
  checking that the verifier rejects it.
- **guard facts** (section 10.6, step 4, "guard facts for bounds checks") — never
  explained; presumably facts that let a check be removed, but that is a guess.
- **UTF-16, UTF-8, code unit** (section 10.3) — used as if known, including in the byte
  calculation, with no definitions in the article or glossary.
- **interpreter** (section 10.4, "the interpreter would still treat every number as a
  general value") — the glossary defines *engine* but not the interpreter inside one.
- **Agenda** and **Files** — used throughout as applications whose ports are being costed,
  but the article never says what either program does, and the glossary has no entries
  for them (only *Compositor*).
- **binding / frontend** (section 10.1 table, "Frontend, WebAssembly linker, RV32
  lowering") — "frontend" and "linker" are not defined; *Lowering* is.

## Claims I could not verify from the article itself

- "Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the
  path to the screen" — no figure, no percentage and no summary of the measurement is
  given here. Since section 10.3's whole proposal is made conditional on that measurement
  ("started only if the key-to-pixel measurement of Article 2 confirms"), the article
  should at least state the number it is relying on.
- "The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step" and "The
  figure of six bytes per unit in step 2 is from the Editor's capacity design note in the
  project's records." — the note is cited but not quoted and is not in the reference list,
  so the six-fold expansion cannot be checked. This matters because it is the evidence
  that step 2 is expensive.
- "Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively, and it costs 660 kB and a
  boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around." — no build time is given, for
  which program, on which device. The 660 kB is repeated from the table but not measured
  in front of the reader; "minutes" is the only performance number and it has no range.
- "Native code about 2.7 times smaller" (step 5 of the roadmap) — the only two numbers the
  article offers give 1,529 / 593 = 2.58, so 2.7 cannot be reproduced. Either the 2.7 comes
  from a different application or the ratio should be "about 2.6".
- "The project's device-language study considered compiling the typed language to
  JavaScript as the way to *run applications fast*, and rejected it for that purpose" — the
  study is not cited in the reference list and its reasoning is only paraphrased in one
  clause, so the reader cannot tell how far the rejection carries over to the new purpose.
- "Twelve applications still to port" — the article never lists the applications or says how
  many exist in total, so the size of the remaining work, which drives step 7's ordering,
  is unverifiable.
- "The typed versions are four to six times longer" — the two factors given are 5.5 and 4.4,
  which is a narrower range than "four to six", and the article does not say what the other
  applications measure. (The two quoted factors themselves check out: 1,730 / 316 = 5.5 and
  (468 + 869) / 307 = 4.4.)
- "Editor contains 104 such `writeLiteral` calls" — plausible and specific, but no way is
  given to confirm it and no second example beyond the one quoted line.
- The asm.js quotation ("by means of an explicit coercion on function entry") and the
  TypeScript 5.8 and TC39 stage-1 claims are attributed to outside sources in the
  reference list; they cannot be checked from the article, and the article does not say
  what a reader should conclude if the stage-1 proposal is withdrawn.

## Section scores

- **10.1** — 4. The inventory table and the size comparison are easy to follow and the two
  multipliers are arithmetically correct, but "four to six times" is looser than the two
  figures given, and the reader is left to work out what "three reactors" counts.
- **10.2** — 4. The diagram makes the three hand-written lists concrete and the failure
  mode is stated plainly, but the passage about the count check leaves the reader to guess
  which two of the three lists it covers, and the WIT paragraph is dense.
- **10.3** — 4. The numbered five-step walkthrough is the clearest passage in the article
  and the byte arithmetic can be checked line by line; it loses a point for the unstated
  field widths and for the unexplained tension with "already native code".
- **10.4** — 3. The rewrite table is genuinely useful, but the asm.js and TypeScript history
  takes three paragraphs to reach it, and the reader is asked to accept the list of
  semantic differences on the authority of Articles 8 and 9 without a summary.
- **10.5** — 4. Removing one mechanism at a time with an explicit condition is easy to
  follow, but the fourth row's "Could be removed when: Now" breaks the column's logic and
  the reader has to reinterpret it as a decision.
- **10.6** — 3. The roadmap table is the most useful artefact in the article, but effort
  classes are only relative, and the flowchart's edges do not match the table's "Unlocks"
  column (step 3 does not list step 10 in the table although the graph draws
  interface description → screen protocol), so a reader cannot tell which of the two to
  trust.
- **10.7** — 4. Every prediction has a check and a consequence, which is exactly what the
  reader needs, but several predictions quote models and counts from earlier articles
  ("the counting model", "71 state fields") that are not described here.
- **10.8** — 5. Six bullets that could serve as the summary of the issue; nothing unclear.
- **10.9** — 4. Five of the six questions can be answered from this article alone; question
  5 requires the reader to connect "no `await`" among three missing features to the 4–6
  times multiplier, which the text never does explicitly.

## Questions that the article did not let me answer

- **Question 1, partly.** The failure the check catches and the failure it misses are both
  stated. What is not stated is which of the three files supplies the header count, so the
  phrase "one list and not the other" has to be interpreted by the reader. It is also never
  said whether the C implementation's order is checked at all, which is one half of "how
  does the interface description remove both".
- **Question 5, partly.** The ordering reason is given ("porting twelve applications in the
  current style would produce a great deal of code that `await` would then make obsolete")
  and the multiplier can be recomputed, but the article never says how much of the 4–6
  times comes from the absence of `await` rather than from the absence of allocation and
  string operations. A reader can quote the ordering but cannot weigh it.
- Questions 2, 3, 4 and 6 are answerable from the text; question 6 needs the reader to
  choose from a table, which is fair, though the "counting model" it refers to is not
  described anywhere in this article.

## One thing to add and one thing to cut

**Add.** A worked example of the interface description: one entry for one reactor function
showing name, parameter types, result type, capability and fuel, next to the three artefacts
generated from it — the compiler table row, the assembly trampoline and the C prototype —
with one sentence on how the *order* is derived. Section 10.2 is the article's most
load-bearing proposal and its smallest, and one example would make both the "one source"
claim and question 1 concrete, instead of leaving the reader to infer where the header
count comes from.

**Cut.** The WIT resource-and-handle aside in 10.2 ("it can declare a *resource* type, an
entity 'that can only be passed around indirectly via handle values', with owned and
borrowed handles…"). It introduces a fourth topic — handle ownership — in a sentence that
already carries the main point that WIT is a precedent, and no step of the roadmap in 10.6
depends on it; the capability and fuel additions that follow are the parts the roadmap
actually needs.

# Investigation entry

## Step 1: Reading the article and the glossary

I read `article.md` once from start to finish without stopping, then read `glossary.md`
term by term looking up the words the article used that I was not sure of, and only then
went back through the article a second time to check the arithmetic and the cross-references
between sections. The article is the tenth in a series, so most of its difficulty comes from
sentences that point at earlier articles rather than from the sentences themselves.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Read TASK.md and carry out every step in order."
**Assistant interpretation:** Read the task file, then do steps 1–4: read the article with the
glossary, answer the quiz, write feedback, write this diary.
**Inferred user intent:** Pre-publication check of a teaching article by a reader who does not
have the earlier nine articles to hand, so that the editor learns where the text fails to
teach rather than where it is merely terse.
**Commit (code):** none — this session produced only prose files.

### What I did
- Read `TASK.md`, `article.md`, `glossary.md`, `diary-format.md`.
- Second pass over `article.md` sections 10.1, 10.3, 10.6 and 10.7 with a calculator:
  1,730/316 = 5.47; (468+869)/307 = 4.35; 17×49 = 833; 833×2 = 1,666; 1,666+17×4 = 1,734;
  1,529/593 = 2.58.
- Looked up in `glossary.md`: world, nucleus, engine, reactor, trampoline, CJI, typed
  compiler, lowering, fuel, verifier, PMP, arena, linear type, typestate, state machine,
  continuation, content key, compile-time operand stack.

### Why
The task asks specifically for terms that *neither* the article *nor* the glossary explains,
so the glossary had to be searched per term rather than skimmed. Checking the arithmetic was
the only way to separate "I did not understand" from "the numbers do not add up".

### What worked
- The glossary covered nearly all of the article's vocabulary: world, engine, reactor,
  trampoline, fuel, verifier, arena, linear type, typestate were all there.
- Most of the article's own arithmetic reproduced exactly (1,666 and 1,734 bytes; 5.5 and
  4.4 multipliers).
- Section 10.3's five-step list was the one passage I could follow without going back.

### What didn't work
- I could not find "firmware", "ELF", "capability", "relocation", "garbage collector",
  "mutation testing", "guard facts", "UTF-16", "code unit", "frontend" or "linker" in the
  glossary, although the article's opening paragraph claims "every term is in the glossary".
  Recovery: I treated them as unexplained and listed them in `feedback.md`.
- "Native code about 2.7 times smaller" in step 5 of the roadmap would not reproduce from
  the two counts given (593 and 1,529, ratio 2.58). Recovery: recorded as an unverifiable
  claim instead of assuming an arithmetic slip.

### What I learned
- The article's difficulty is concentrated in noun phrases built from the earlier articles
  ("the counting model", "71 state fields", "the key-to-pixel measurement"), not in its own
  definitions, which are mostly careful.
- A claim of the form "every term is in the glossary" is itself checkable, and this one is
  not quite true — a useful thing to report to an editor.

### What was tricky to build
Understanding section 10.2 took the longest. Three files must agree; the diagram shows a
proposed single source generating all three; but the check described afterwards compares a
header count against *one* table only. The text never says which file holds the header count,
so I had to reason from the trampoline description ("one jump per function, in the same
order") that the count must belong to the assembly side, and that the C file is simply
unchecked — a gap the interface description closes but the article does not name.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Whether "four structural changes" is meant to include section 10.5, since the article never
  says which four it counts.
- Whether the flowchart in 10.6 is meant to agree with the "Unlocks" column of the roadmap
  table; they differ over step 3 → step 10.

### What should be done in the future
- N/A for this session; the follow-ups belong to the editor (see the "Add/Cut" pair in
  `feedback.md`).

### Code review instructions
- Read `answers.md` against sections 10.2, 10.3, 10.4, 10.1 and 10.7 of `article.md`; every
  answer quotes only this article.
- Check `feedback.md`'s arithmetic: 1,529/593 = 2.58, not "about 2.7".

### Technical details
- Files read: `TASK.md`, `article.md` (~200 lines), `glossary.md`, `diary-format.md`.
- Files written: `answers.md`, `feedback.md`, `diary.md`.
- No code was compiled or run.

## Step 2: Answering the quiz

I answered the six questions in `answers.md`, numbered as in the article, keeping each answer
between two and six sentences, showing the multipliers and byte counts as working, and adding
a `Confidence:` line after each.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** see Step 1
**Assistant interpretation:** Answer questions 1–6 of section 10.9 in my own words, with
working where a calculation is asked for, and self-report confidence 1–5.
**Inferred user intent:** Test whether the article actually teaches enough to answer its own
questions, and to see which answers had to be reconstructed rather than read off.
**Commit (code):** none.

### What I did
- Wrote six answers to `answers.md`; four quote a section directly, two recompute numbers
  (question 5 the 5.5 and 4.4 multipliers; question 6 the 1,529/593 ratio).
- Assigned confidences 5, 5, 5, 4, 4, 5.

### Why
The confidence line is the only place where I can record the difference between an answer I
found in the text and one I inferred from it, which is the difference the editor cares about.

### What worked
- Questions 2, 3 and 6 were directly answerable: the five steps, the rewrite table and the
  predictions table each supply the whole answer.
- Question 1's two named failures ("catches", "cannot catch") are stated in one sentence
  each, so quoting was enough.

### What didn't work
- Question 5 needed a step the article does not take: it lists three missing features
  (allocation, string operations, `await`) as the cause of the 4–6 times multiplier, then
  orders `await` before the ports because of that multiplier, without saying how much of the
  multiplier `await` accounts for. Recovery: I recomputed the multipliers, quoted the
  ordering sentence, and lowered my confidence to 4.
- Question 4 has an awkward edge I could not settle from the text: a bug in the *emitter*
  would also produce a screen mismatch, so "detects an error in the backend" is right but
  incomplete about how the two mismatch kinds would be told apart. I said so in the answer.

### What I learned
- Answering question 1 exposed that "one interface description removes both" is an
  argument the article makes in one clause; a reader has to reconstruct why generation, and
  not comparison, is what fixes the ordering problem.

### What was tricky to build
Question 6 requires naming the observation that refutes a prediction. The table gives a
"Check" and an "If it fails" column but no threshold for the first row, so "what observation
would refute it" had to be phrased as "a count well above 593 and near 1,529" — the article
supplies the comparison but leaves the margin to the reader.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Answer 4's remark about distinguishing emitter bugs from backend bugs is my own addition;
  an editor should confirm the article does not intend to address it.

### What should be done in the future
- N/A.

### Code review instructions
- Compare each answer with the section it cites; confirm no answer relies on an earlier
  article of the series.

### Technical details
- `answers.md`: 6 numbered answers, each ending in `Confidence: N`.

## Step 3: Writing the feedback

I wrote `feedback.md` with the six requested sections: passages I had to read twice (seven
quotations with the reason), terms used before explanation or never explained (eleven
entries), claims I could not verify (nine quotations), scores for sections 10.1–10.9, the
questions the article did not let me answer, and one thing to add and one to cut.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** see Step 1
**Assistant interpretation:** Report honestly where the article fails to teach, quoting rather
than paraphrasing, and score each numbered section 1–5 with one sentence of reason.
**Inferred user intent:** An actionable pre-publication review: exact quotations so the
editor can find the sentence, and a distinction between "hard for me" and "missing".
**Commit (code):** none.

### What I did
- `feedback.md`, six headed sections matching the task's wording.
- Scored: 10.1 = 4, 10.2 = 4, 10.3 = 4, 10.4 = 3, 10.5 = 4, 10.6 = 3, 10.7 = 4, 10.8 = 5,
  10.9 = 4.
- Cross-checked every listed term against `glossary.md` before writing the line, and dropped
  those the glossary actually defines (world, engine, reactor, trampoline, fuel, verifier,
  PMP, arena, typestate, continuation).
- Proposed adding a worked interface-description example and cutting the WIT
  resource/handle aside.

### Why
Quotation plus one line of diagnosis is the only form the editor can act on; a general
impression ("dense") would be useless. For add/cut I chose the smallest change that repairs
the section the quiz leans on most (10.2) and the passage that carries no roadmap weight.

### What worked
- The arithmetic checks gave objective findings: the 2.7-versus-2.58 discrepancy, and the
  "four to six times" range being wider than the 4.4 and 5.5 actually quoted.
- The glossary-vs-article term sweep produced a concrete list; "firmware" in the very first
  sentence is not defined in either file.

### What didn't work
- The task asks to report only terms that *neither* the article *nor* the glossary explains,
  and for a few entries I am not fully sure the article does not explain them in passing —
  "capability" is used once and might be meant to be the glossary's *Claim*. I listed it with
  that doubt stated rather than silently dropping it. Recovery: noted in the line itself.
- I could not decide which of the article's internal cross-references are deliberate
  forward-references and which are omissions, so the "claims I could not verify" section
  sticks to quoting and naming the missing figure.

### What I learned
- Most of my reading difficulty was not vocabulary but unstated quantities: the article
  argues from measurements in other articles without ever restating one of them, which makes
  its own conditionals ("started only if the measurement confirms") impossible for a reader
  of this article to evaluate.

### What was tricky to build
Keeping the "passages I had to read twice" section honest was the hard part. Some sentences
were hard because they are genuinely unclear (the nested fuel/capability sentence) and some
because I lacked the earlier articles (the 71 state fields). Mixing them would mislead the
editor, so I recorded the second kind under unverifiable claims and cross-references and
labelled it as such inside the entry.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- The section score of 3 for 10.6 rests on the flowchart/table mismatch over step 3 → step
  10; if the graph is meant to show only the strongest dependencies, the score should rise.
- The "cut" recommendation removes a sentence that justifies part of the description
  format; an editor may prefer to shorten rather than cut it.

### What should be done in the future
- If the article is revised, restate Article 2's key-to-pixel figure and Article 8's state
  field count in this text, since both are now load-bearing for the roadmap's ordering.

### Code review instructions
- Check each quoted passage against `article.md` (search the distinctive phrase) and each
  term against `glossary.md`; the claim that a term is missing should be reproducible by
  searching both files.
- Re-run the two ratios: 1,730/316 = 5.47 and 1,529/593 = 2.58.

### Technical details
- `feedback.md`: 7 passages, 11 terms, 9 unverifiable claims, 9 section scores, 2 partly
  unanswerable quiz questions, 1 add, 1 cut.
- Terms searched in both files and found missing: firmware, ELF, capability, relocation,
  garbage collector, mutation testing, guard facts, UTF-16/UTF-8/code unit, interpreter,
  Agenda/Files, frontend/linker.
